column2: The Anxiety of Impermanence and the Impermanence of Anxiety
Ajahn Pasanno leads a day of teaching and meditation exploring impermanence and how it can be contemplated in a way that leads to the end of suffering rather than causing anxiety.

You study the teachings of the Buddha this much (gestures short) and practice this much (gestures long).|Ajahn Chah
Could you talk about how attachment relates to the theme [of the day]?

Could you talk about the phrase attributed to Ajahn Chah, 'the one who knows?' You said to learn the difference between the one who knows and the mind objects. Are you talking about a pure awareness? I don't usually associate that with the mind, but maybe it is?
What you have to know is the knowledge and intention that brought you here in the first place to ask that question.|Ajahn Buddhadāsa

This morning I kept drowsing off in meditation. I eventually just gave in because I felt like, 'Well, if that's what my mind needs, I'm going to do that.' I came here to practice and have an experience of concentration and maybe insight and instead I had sleepiness to the max. In this case, is it wisdom to accept sleepiness or is there a trick?

My experience in the world lately has been troublesome with the number of hateful things people seem to be doing to each other now. As an individual, I sit in this room, and we're all of one mind, and we can nap or we can munch, or we can talk about our practice. But I don't know how to bring it out there, and I really don't know how to decrease my anxiety over the ugliness of some of our human behavior.
Snp 2.4: Maṅgala Sutta (Chanting Book p. 46).
Could you expand on the difference between the sense of no-self versus annihilation of the self and tie this in to the concept of suññatā?

There's impermanence that is more obvious to a human being in terms of how we exist. So a rainbow appears, we know it's just temporary, we appreciate that, and it disappears [when] the causes and conditions change. What's harder is things that occur over the course of a lifetime that we tend to see as permanent. Could you offer any reflection on time frames of impermanence and how we can engage with those longer things that seem so permanent?
How in the face of impermanence do we understand the concept of the unborn?
I experience anxiety as excruciatingly physical. How can I be more skillful with this discomfort?
Could you talk about the void? Is that unborn, unconditional element of pure potential?
MN 121: The Lesser Discourse on Emptiness.

With great respect and listening carefully, I'm having a hard time. I have looked at impermanence for a long time, but once I got older and turned 70, I see clearly that things I would have grasped at and thought would make me happy will not. They all change or they pass and go away. I know that I want to control, and I see that that's not there. I just fractured my back, so my body is not a place where I have control. If I meditate and get out of thoughts, I have less suffering, but I don't really have much happiness; I simply have less suffering. I see and am close to many people who have meditated a lot longer than I have. I don't mean to be judgemental, but I don't see them much happier than I am. It's discouraging. ...
I definitely don't take my refuge as my body or even the mind of the intellect.
Luang Ta Mahā Boowa forgets what he has said during a Dhamma talk shortly after Ajahn Chah's death.
Could you speak about what attachment looks like in intimate relationships? We're conditioned in many ways to relate to such relationships with a certain level of grasping.
Could you talk about the way you use the word refuge? In colloquial English, this comes up only as refugees, but apparently it's a common word in your circle.
But you also say that it's a mistake to take refuge in your body, mind or bank account, all the thing we normally look to for safety.
From your own experience, could you describe a story of skillful non-acceptance? I am always trying to find the middle way between acceptance and trying to change things.
What is the role of impermanence in karma as it is coming to fruition?

When to accept things as they are? Or when to say, 'This is unacceptable' or 'I don't want this in my life?' Like I don't want to be continually chasing the dollar in the Bay Area as prices go up and things get crazy here. ... This is not the life I want. I don't know how to use Buddhism skillfully; I feel a little oppressed by, 'Oh, well it's just causes and conditions, so I should really just be happy with what I have.' Where do you go with that?

Being that we have little or no control over most thoughts and emotions, how are we to understand the instructions to discipline our body, speech, and mind? Where do we put our hopes that we can accomplish that?
